# Three ways to index a vector

Postgres can index a `vector` column in three ways, with pgvector's **HNSW**, Timescale's **DiskANN**
from pgvectorscale, or **PRISM** from the newer pg_vectorsearch. On 20,000 random 64-dimensional
vectors, PRISM built nine times faster than HNSW at a sixth of the size and nearly matched its
recall, while DiskANN stalled at 0.76. Random vectors are the worst case for DiskANN and PRISM, so
these numbers rank the indexes under stress. On real embeddings, which cluster strongly, both should
do better, though the lab did not measure that.

## Index designs

**HNSW** (pgvector) is a layered proximity graph. A query enters at the sparse top layer and
descends towards the dense bottom one, keeping `ef_search` candidates as it goes, so it needs no
training pass and inserts stay cheap. Its two settings, `m` (the links per node) and
`ef_construction`, trade build time for recall.

**DiskANN** (pgvectorscale 0.9.1) is a single flat graph, built to stay fast when it does not fit in
memory. It keeps compressed vectors in the index (statistical binary quantization) and re-reads the
full vectors only to rescore the best candidates.

**PRISM** (pg_vectorsearch 0.1.0, alpha, Postgres 18 only) partitions instead of walking a graph.
k-means splits the table into `nlist` partitions, in the style of an IVF index, and stores each
vector as a RaBitQ code with an error bound. A query scans the `prism.nprobe` nearest partitions and
re-reads full vectors only for the candidates the error bound cannot settle. Because PRISM indexes
pgvector's column in place, creating and tuning it takes three statements:

```sql
CREATE INDEX ON demo_docs USING prism (embedding vec32_cosine_ops);  -- build after loading
SET prism.nprobe = 40;                                               -- 0 = auto
SELECT * FROM prism_index_settings('demo_docs_embedding_idx');       -- what it chose, and why
```

## Build time and recall

The test ran once on a laptop, on Postgres 18, and measured recall@10 (how many of the exact top 10
the index returns) against an exact scan:

| index | build | size | best recall@10 | ms per query at best |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| HNSW (m 16, ef_construction 64) | 2.7 s | 11.4 MB | 0.99 (ef_search 400) | 3.3 |
| DiskANN (defaults) | 20.3 s | 9.1 MB | 0.76 (search list 400, rescore 400) | 8.3 |
| PRISM (auto nlist 144) | 0.3 s | 1.8 MB | 0.98 (nprobe 160, every list) | 3.0 |

PRISM's recall nearly matches HNSW's once every partition is probed. The automatic `nprobe` (10
here) reaches only about 0.40, and recall rises to 0.81 at 40 and 0.93 at 80.

::: {.callout-important}
## The test data

Random vectors are the worst case for both quantization and partitioning. Their coordinates are
independent, so binary codes have nothing to capture and k-means has no clusters to follow. That is
why DiskANN stalls at 0.76 and PRISM needs every partition. Real embeddings cluster strongly, and on
them both indexes should do far better, though the lab did not measure that. PRISM's automatic `nprobe` aims at a recall of about 0.95.
:::

## Choosing an index

Use HNSW unless something rules it out, since it needs no training, is mature, and gives good
recall at any size that fits in memory. DiskANN suits an index that will not fit in RAM, if the
slower build is affordable. PRISM suits frequent rebuilds or many tables, where build time and size
matter, as long as you are on Postgres 18 and accept that an alpha may need `DROP EXTENSION` and a
rebuild between releases. In SQLAlchemy all three are an `Index(...)` with `postgresql_using` and
`postgresql_ops`, and the queries stay the same.
